Metals.q: An unknown element is shiny, bends without breaking and conducts electricity. What is it most likely?
wrong: Nonmetals are brittle and poor conductors.
Metalloids have only some metallic properties; this one shows all of them.
Noble gases are gases, not shiny solids that bend.
Metals.exp: Shiny, bendable and conductive are metal properties.

Metals.q: Element Q sits to the left of the staircase in period 4. Which set of properties should it have?
wrong: Brittle, dull and a poor conductor of both heat and electricity
Those are nonmetal properties, found right of the staircase.
Some metal and some nonmetal traits
That's a metalloid, on the staircase.
A gas that forms no ions
That's a noble gas, in column 18.
Metals.exp: Left of the staircase means metal: good conductors that bend and draw into wires.

Malleable.q: A gold bar is hammered into a sheet thinner than paper. Which property does this show?
wrong: Ductility is being drawn into wire, not hammered into sheets.
Conductivity is about carrying heat or electricity.
Malleable.exp: Being hammered or bent into shape is malleability.

Malleable.q: A worker hammers a sample and it flattens into a sheet; a second sample shatters. What can you conclude?
Malleable.right: The first is likely a metal; the second a nonmetal
wrong: Both are metals, since every element will change shape if it is hit hard
Malleable.exp: Malleability (hammered into sheets) is a metal property; nonmetals are brittle.

Ductile.q: Copper is pulled through a die to make electrical wire. Which property makes that possible?
wrong: Malleability is being hammered into sheets, not drawn into wire.
A brittle material would snap instead of stretching.
Density has nothing to do with being drawn into wire.
Ductile.exp: Being drawn out into wire is ductility.

Ductile.q: Why are electrical wires made from metals and not from sulfur?
Ductile.right: Metals can be drawn into wires and conduct
wrong: Sulfur is too heavy to hang from poles, even though it conducts well
Sulfur is a brittle nonmetal and a poor conductor.
Ductile.exp: Metals are ductile and good conductors; nonmetals like sulfur are brittle and poor conductors.

Nonmetals.q: Sulfur is yellow, shatters when struck and does not conduct electricity. Where is it on the table?
wrong: That is where the metals are; metals do not shatter.
Metalloids have some metallic properties; sulfur has none.
Those are the inner transition metals.
Nonmetals.exp: Brittle and nonconducting means nonmetal, right of the staircase.

Nonmetals.q: Hydrogen sits on the left side of the table. Why is it still grouped with the nonmetals?
wrong: It is a metal, because every element on the left side of the table is a metal
Nonmetals.exp: Nonmetals sit right of the staircase, plus hydrogen, even though it's on the left.

Metalloids.q: Which element has some metallic and some nonmetallic properties?
wrong: Aluminum touches the staircase but is a metal.
Metalloids.exp: Silicon sits on the staircase: a metalloid.

Metalloids.q: Aluminum touches the staircase. A student calls it a metalloid. What's the correction?
wrong: The student is right, since anything touching the staircase is a metalloid
Your slide makes aluminum the exception.
Metalloids.exp: Aluminum touches the staircase but is a metal; the metalloids on your slide are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te.

Group.q: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium react in similar ways?
wrong: They are in different periods, so they have different numbers of shells.
Each element has a different number of protons.
Their atomic masses are very different.
Group.exp: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.

Group.q: Why do fluorine and chlorine react in similar ways?
wrong: They are in the same row, so they have the same number of electron shells
Same row means same shells, not similar behavior.
They have the same number of protons
Then they'd be the same element.
Group.exp: Elements in one group share the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike.

Alkali metals.q: Which element is an alkali metal?
wrong: Hydrogen sits in group 1 but is a nonmetal.
Magnesium is in group 2, the alkaline earth metals.
Alkali metals.exp: Potassium is in group 1, below hydrogen.

Alkali metals.q: Hydrogen is at the top of column 1. Is it an alkali metal?
wrong: Yes, because every element in the first column is counted as an alkali metal
That's not true of hydrogen or group 1.
Alkali metals.exp: Alkali metals are group 1, not counting hydrogen.

Alkaline earth metals.q: Strontium is in group 2. What charge does its ion have?
wrong: Only noble gases tend not to form ions.

Alkaline earth metals.q: Element M forms an M²⁺ ion and sits on the left of the table. Which family is it most likely in?
wrong: Alkali metals, because they are the metals found on the far left of the table
Alkaline earth metals.exp: Column 2, the alkaline earth metals, form +2 ions.

Transition metals.q: Why might a question about iron's ion need to tell you its charge?
wrong: Iron does form ions: Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
Iron is a metal in the transition block.
Iron's charge varies; 1+ is the alkali metal charge.
Transition metals.exp: Transition metals in groups 3 to 12 often have variable charges.

Transition metals.q: Copper can form Cu⁺ or Cu²⁺. Where is copper on the table?
wrong: Group 1, since it can form a +1 ion just like sodium and potassium
Variable charges point to the transition metals.
Transition metals.exp: Transition metals (groups 3 to 12) often have variable charges.

Halogens.q: Bromine is a halogen. What ion does it form?
wrong: Halogens gain an electron; they do not lose one.
2- ions come from group 16, not group 17.
Only noble gases tend not to form ions.
Halogens.exp: Group 17 gains one electron to complete its octet.

Halogens.q: Element X is in the same family as chlorine. What formula would its compound with sodium have?
wrong: Na₂X, because the halogen needs to take two electrons to fill its octet
Halogens form -1 ions, so one Na⁺ balances one.
Halogens.exp: Halogens form -1 ions; Na⁺ and X⁻ combine 1:1.

Noble gases.q: Why does argon not form ions?
wrong: It has no electrons at all
Noble gases.exp: Group 18 already has a complete valence shell.

Noble gases.q: Which element would be least likely to appear in an ionic compound?
wrong: Sodium, because it has only a single electron in its outer energy level
Noble gases.exp: Noble gases already have a full valence shell, so they tend not to form ions.

Inner transition metals.q: Where are the inner transition metals on the periodic table?
wrong: That column is group 18, the noble gases.
That is the main transition metal block.
Inner transition metals.exp: They are the lanthanide and actinide rows set below the table.

Inner transition metals.q: Why are two rows set apart below the main periodic table?
wrong: They are the noble gases, which are kept apart because they rarely react
Inner transition metals.exp: The lanthanide and actinide series are the inner transition metals, set below the table.

Lanthanide series.q: Which atomic numbers make up the lanthanide series?
wrong: Those are group numbers for the transition metals.
Those are group numbers, not atomic numbers.
Actinide series, because all of the elements below the main table are actinides
Lanthanide series.exp: The lanthanide series runs from atomic number 58 to 71.

Actinide series.q: The actinide series is named after which element?
wrong: Uranium is in the series but does not name it.
There is no element called actinide.

Actinide series.q: Element 92 is in which row below the table?
wrong: The lanthanide series, which holds the inner transition metals from 58 to 71
That holds only H and He.
Actinide series.exp: The actinide series runs from 90 to 103.

Period.q: Sodium is in period 3. How many electron shells (energy levels) does it have?
wrong: 1 is its number of valence electrons (group 1).
8 is a full octet, not a shell count.
Period.exp: The period number gives the number of energy levels.

Period.q: Potassium and bromine are in the same period. What do they share?
Period.right: The same number of electron shells
wrong: The same number of valence electrons, so they react in very similar ways
That's shared by a group, not a period.
Then they'd be the same element.
Period.exp: Elements in one row have the same number of electron shells.

States at room temperature.q: At 25 °C, how many elements on the periodic table are liquids?
wrong: Two elements are liquids at room temperature.

States at room temperature.q: At 25 °C, how many elements on the periodic table are gases?
wrong: 2, the same as the number of elements that are liquids at room temperature
States at room temperature.exp: At 25 °C there are 11 gases and 2 liquids; everything else is solid.

wrong: That was Rutherford, about 2,300 years later.
Leucippus.exp: Leucippus and a partner proposed that matter is made of tiny particles.

Leucippus.q: Which later word comes from the idea Leucippus and his partner proposed?
wrong: Nucleus, since they said matter has a tiny dense center that holds its mass
Leucippus.exp: Leucippus proposed that matter is made of tiny particles, the idea behind the word atom.

Antoine Lavoisier.q: Wood burns and the ash weighs less, but nothing is truly lost. Whose idea explains this?
Antoine Lavoisier.exp: Lavoisier: matter is not created or destroyed, only changed in form.

Antoine Lavoisier.q: A sealed jar with steel wool is weighed before and after the steel wool burns. The mass doesn't change. Which idea does this support?
wrong: Matter is made of electrons scattered through a sphere of positive charge
Antoine Lavoisier.exp: Lavoisier: matter can't be created or destroyed, only change form (conservation of mass).

Dalton's atomic theory (1810).q: In a reaction, the atoms are rearranged into new substances. Which theory says this?
wrong: Bohr's model is about where electrons are.
Thomson's model describes the inside of an atom, not reactions.
Heisenberg's work is about predicting electron positions.
Dalton's atomic theory (1810).exp: Dalton said atoms are not created or destroyed, only regrouped.

Dalton's atomic theory (1810).q: Which statement is part of Dalton's theory?
Dalton's atomic theory (1810).right: Atoms of one element are identical
wrong: Atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus
That's isotopes, found later; Dalton said identical.
Dalton's atomic theory (1810).exp: Dalton said atoms of a given element are identical (later revised by the discovery of isotopes).

Law of constant composition.q: Water from a lake and water from a lab both have 2 H for every O. Which law is this?
wrong: That law is about mass not being created or destroyed.
That is about atoms not splitting in reactions.
That is about atoms completing their valence shells.
Law of constant composition.exp: A compound always has the same atoms in the same ratio.

Law of constant composition.q: A sample of carbon dioxide has 1 C for every 2 O. Another sample from a car's exhaust is tested. What will it show?
wrong: A different ratio, because the exhaust comes from a different source than the lab
A compound always has the same ratio.
Law of constant composition.exp: A given compound always has the same relative numbers and types of atoms.

J. J. Thomson (1897).q: Which discovery belongs to J. J. Thomson?
J. J. Thomson (1897).exp: Thomson used cathode ray tubes to find tiny negative particles.

J. J. Thomson (1897).q: Thomson found negative particles in atoms. Why did he decide atoms must also hold positive charge?
wrong: He saw positive particles bounce off a gold foil target during an experiment
J. J. Thomson (1897).exp: To balance the electrons, so atoms are neutral overall.

Plum pudding model.q: In the plum pudding model, what are the 'plums'?
wrong: The positive charge is the pudding, spread throughout.
Neutrons had not been discovered yet.
The plum pudding model has no nucleus.
Plum pudding model.exp: Negative electrons were scattered in a ball of positive charge.

Plum pudding model.q: Which experiment showed the plum pudding model was wrong?
wrong: Thomson's cathode ray tube experiment, which first found the electrons inside atoms
That led to the plum pudding model.
That came before electrons were known.
Plum pudding model.exp: Rutherford's results disproved the plum pudding model.

Ernest Rutherford (1911).q: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did Rutherford conclude?
wrong: Solid atoms would stop or bounce most particles.
Neutrons were found later by Chadwick.
Ernest Rutherford (1911).exp: Particles passing straight through means mostly empty space.

Ernest Rutherford (1911).q: A few alpha particles bounced straight back from the foil. What did that show?
wrong: The atom is mostly empty space, so particles can pass through it freely
That came from the particles that went straight through.
Ernest Rutherford (1911).exp: Particles bouncing back showed a small, dense, positive nucleus.

Nucleus.q: Where is almost all of an atom's mass?
wrong: Rutherford showed the mass is packed in a tiny center.
Nucleus.exp: Protons and neutrons, which have mass, are in the nucleus.

Nucleus.q: An atom's nucleus takes up a tiny space. Why is the atom's mass still mostly there?
Nucleus.right: The protons and neutrons are there
wrong: The electrons are in the nucleus, and they are the heaviest particles of all
Electrons are outside and nearly massless.
Neutrons have about the same mass.
Nucleus.exp: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, so nearly all the mass.

James Chadwick (1932).q: Chadwick's neutral radiation from beryllium turned out to be what?
wrong: Alpha particles were what he fired, not what he found.
James Chadwick (1932).exp: Neutral particles with about a proton's mass: neutrons.

James Chadwick (1932).q: Before Chadwick, what was missing from the picture of the nucleus?
wrong: The electron, which no one had yet found in any experiment on atoms
Rutherford had shown a positive center.
Orbits are Bohr's idea, about electrons.
James Chadwick (1932).exp: Chadwick's neutron completed the picture of the nucleus.

Niels Bohr (1913).q: Which model shows electrons circling the nucleus like planets around the sun?
wrong: Thomson's model has no nucleus to circle.
Dalton's atoms had no inner parts.
Orbitals are likely regions, not planet-like paths.
Niels Bohr (1913).exp: Bohr placed electrons in fixed orbits.

Niels Bohr (1913).q: How did Bohr's model differ from Rutherford's?
wrong: A uniform sphere of positive charge with the electrons scattered inside it
Niels Bohr (1913).exp: Bohr placed electrons in orbits that are fixed energy levels.

Energy level.q: Chlorine is in period 3. How many energy levels does its Bohr model need?
wrong: 7 is chlorine's number of valence electrons.
Chlorine has more than one shell; period 3 means 3.
Energy level.exp: The period number gives the number of energy levels.

Energy level.q: Potassium is in period 4. How many energy levels does its Bohr model have?
wrong: 1, because potassium is in group 1 and has only one valence electron
The group gives valence electrons; the period gives levels.
Energy level.exp: The period number tells how many energy levels an atom has.

Problem with Bohr's model.q: What is wrong with Bohr's model of the atom?
wrong: It puts electrons in the nucleus
Bohr placed electrons outside the nucleus, in orbits.
Bohr's electrons are negative, as they should be.
Bohr's model includes protons in the nucleus.
Problem with Bohr's model.exp: We cannot know exactly where an electron is.

Problem with Bohr's model.q: Why was Bohr's model replaced by orbitals?
Problem with Bohr's model.right: We can't know an electron's exact path
wrong: Electrons were found to sit inside the nucleus alongside the protons
Problem with Bohr's model.exp: Electrons don't follow exact orbits; we can't know exactly where one is.

Orbitals (modern model).q: In the modern model, where is an electron found?
wrong: That is closer to Thomson's model.
Orbitals (modern model).exp: Orbitals are regions where an electron is likely to be about 90% of the time.

Orbitals (modern model).q: In the modern model, what does an orbital show?
Orbitals (modern model).right: Where an electron is likely to be
wrong: The exact circular path that each electron always follows around the nucleus
Orbitals (modern model).exp: An orbital is a region where an electron is found about 90% of the time.

Proton.q: Which particle is positive and found in the nucleus?
wrong: Neutrons are in the nucleus but have no charge.
Electrons are negative and outside the nucleus.
An ion is a whole charged atom, not a particle inside one.

Proton.q: Two atoms each have 9 protons but different masses. What do you know for sure?
wrong: They are different elements, because atoms with different masses can't match
They have the same mass number
They have the same number of neutrons
Different masses mean different neutron counts.
Proton.exp: The number of protons decides the element.

Neutron.q: Which particle is in the nucleus but has no charge?
wrong: Electrons are negative and outside the nucleus.
A cation is a positive ion, not a particle.

Neutron.q: Adding a neutron to an atom changes which of these?
wrong: Its charge, because the neutron brings an extra positive charge into the nucleus
Neutron.exp: A neutron adds mass (about a proton's) but no charge.

Electron.q: Which particle is nearly massless and found outside the nucleus?
wrong: Protons have mass and are in the nucleus.
Neutrons have mass and are in the nucleus.
The nucleus holds almost all the mass.

Electron.q: An atom loses an electron. What happens to its mass?
wrong: It drops by about the same amount as losing one proton from the nucleus
Electron.exp: Electrons are nearly massless, so losing one barely changes the mass.

Number of protons.q: An atom gains a proton. What happens?
wrong: Ions form from gaining or losing electrons.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not protons.
Changing protons changes the atomic number.
Number of protons.exp: The number of protons sets which element it is.

Number of protons.q: A nucleus changes from 6 protons to 7. What has the atom become?
wrong: A heavier isotope of carbon, since only the mass of the atom has changed
Number of protons.exp: Change the proton count and you have a different element: 7 protons is nitrogen.

Number of electrons.q: Which change would affect how an atom bonds?
wrong: Neutrons make isotopes, which react almost the same.
Mass number counts nucleus particles, which do not bond.
Number of electrons.exp: Chemical behavior comes from the electrons.

Number of electrons.q: Na and Na⁺ have the same nucleus. Why do they behave so differently?
Number of electrons.right: They have different numbers of electrons
wrong: They have different numbers of protons, so they are really different elements
They have different numbers of neutrons

Atomic number (Z).q: An atom has 26 protons. What is its atomic number?
wrong: That doubles the protons; atomic number is just the protons.
30 would be its neutron count for Fe-56, not its atomic number.
Atomic number (Z).exp: Atomic number = number of protons. 26 is iron.

Atomic number (Z).q: An atom has atomic number 17. Which is true?
wrong: It has 17 neutrons, because the atomic number counts the particles in the nucleus
Atomic number (Z).exp: The atomic number is the number of protons.

Mass number (A).q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
An atom of mass number 40 has 20 neutrons. How many protons does it have?
wrong: 60, because you add the neutrons to the mass number to get the protons
Mass number = protons + neutrons, so subtract.

Neutron count.q: How many neutrons are in ³⁵₁₇Cl?
Sodium's atomic mass is 22.99 and Z = 11. If no isotope is given, how many neutrons does sodium have?
wrong: 11.99, found by subtracting the atomic number from the atomic mass as written

Electrons in a neutral atom.q: How many electrons are in a neutral magnesium atom (Z = 12)?
wrong: 10 is for Mg²⁺, which lost 2 electrons.
Electrons in a neutral atom.exp: Neutral atoms have as many electrons as protons.

Electrons in a neutral atom.q: A neutral atom has 15 electrons. Which element is it? (P is Z = 15)
wrong: Sulfur, because a neutral atom always has one more electron than protons
Electrons in a neutral atom.exp: In a neutral atom electrons = protons, so 15 electrons means Z = 15.

Electrons in an ion.q: How many electrons are in O²⁻ (Z = 8)?
wrong: Subtracting 2 is for a positive ion; O²⁻ gained 2.
8 is for a neutral oxygen atom.

Electrons in an ion.q: How many electrons are in Al³⁺ (Z = 13)?
wrong: 16, because a positive ion gains three electrons to get its charge

Valence electrons.q: Nitrogen is in group 15. How many valence electrons does it have?
wrong: Use the last digit of groups 13-18: group 15 means 5.
3 is how many it gains to form N³⁻.

Valence electrons.q: Sulfur (group 16) and oxygen (group 16) have how many valence electrons each?
wrong: 16, because the group number is the number of valence electrons for every element

Bohr model drawing.q: A Bohr model of magnesium (period 3, group 2) has how many rings and outer electrons?
wrong: Swapped: the period gives rings, the group gives outer electrons.
12 is the total electrons, not the outer ones.
There is one ring per energy level, not per electron.
Bohr model drawing.exp: Period 3 gives 3 rings; group 2 gives 2 valence electrons.

Bohr model drawing.q: A Bohr model has 2 rings and 7 electrons on the outer ring. Which element is it?
wrong: Chlorine, because it is the halogen that has seven electrons in its outer ring
Bohr model drawing.exp: 2 rings = period 2; 7 outer electrons = group 17: fluorine.

Octet.q: Why does chlorine gain one electron when it forms an ion?
wrong: Only H and He are complete with 2.
Gaining an electron makes it negative, not neutral.
Octet.exp: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons; one more completes the octet.

Octet.q: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. What does it tend to do to complete its octet?
wrong: Lose 6 electrons, since losing them leaves an empty and stable outer shell
Octet.exp: Oxygen gains 2 electrons to reach 8, forming O²⁻.

Atomic mass.q: Carbon's atomic mass is 12.011. Why isn't it exactly 12?
wrong: The decimal is real: it is a weighted average.
The decimal comes from the isotope mix.
Atomic mass.exp: Atomic mass is a weighted average of all of an element's isotopes.

Atomic mass.q: Why does a periodic table square show 24.31 for magnesium instead of a whole number?
wrong: It is the number of protons plus electrons in one magnesium atom
That would be a whole number.
Atomic mass.exp: Atomic mass is the average of all isotopes, weighted by how common each is.

Isotopes.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 have the same number of what?
Isotopes.exp: Isotopes have the same protons and different neutrons.

Isotopes.q: Which pair are isotopes of each other?
wrong: Argon-40 and calcium-40, since they have exactly the same mass number
That's an atom and its ion.
Isotopes.exp: Isotopes are the same element with different mass numbers.

Chemistry of isotopes.q: Why do carbon-12 and carbon-14 react the same way?
wrong: They have different numbers of neutrons.
Charge is not what makes reactions alike; electrons are.
Chemistry of isotopes.exp: Chemistry depends on electrons, which isotopes share.

Chemistry of isotopes.q: Water made with deuterium instead of hydrogen-1 still reacts like water. Why?
wrong: Deuterium has an extra proton, which keeps the charges and reactions the same
Deuterium has an extra neutron, not proton.
Chemistry of isotopes.exp: Reactions depend on electrons, not neutrons.

Isotopes in nature.q: Why is chlorine's atomic mass 35.45 and not a whole number?
Isotopes in nature.right: It is a mix of isotopes
wrong: Every atom has a whole number of neutrons.
Then its mass would be close to 35.0.
Isotopes in nature.exp: Natural chlorine is a mixture of isotopes.

Isotopes in nature.q: A sample of copper from a mine contains atoms of different mass numbers. Is that unusual?
Isotopes in nature.right: No; elements are usually mixtures of isotopes
wrong: Yes, because every atom of one element must have exactly the same mass
Yes; it must be two elements
Isotopes in nature.exp: Elements are usually found as a mixture of isotopes.

Isotopic notation.q: In ¹⁴₆C, what does the 6 tell you?
wrong: The mass number is the top number, 14.
Charge goes at the upper right; there is none here.
Isotopic notation.exp: The bottom number is the atomic number: protons.

Isotopic notation.q: An isotope is written ⁵⁶₂₆Fe. How many neutrons does it have?
wrong: 56, which is the top number and counts every particle in the nucleus

Hyphen notation.q: How is ⁴¹₂₀Ca written in hyphen notation?
wrong: 20 is the atomic number; hyphen notation uses the mass number.
The atomic number, which is the number of protons in each uranium atom
Hyphen notation gives the mass number.
You'd subtract Z to get that.
Hyphen notation.exp: Hyphen notation is the element name plus the mass number.

Same element test.q: Which pair is the same element?
wrong: Same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Different atomic numbers mean different elements.
Different atomic numbers mean different elements.
Same element test.exp: Same bottom number (Z = 7) means same element.

Same element test.q: Do ⁴⁰₁₈X and ⁴⁰₂₀X show the same element?
wrong: Yes, because they have exactly the same mass number written on top
Equal mass numbers don't make the same element.
X is a placeholder; Z decides.
Same element test.exp: Two symbols match only if they share an atomic number.

Relative (percent) abundance.q: Boron is 80% boron-11. What does the 80% mean?
wrong: Abundance is a share of atoms, not a mass.
Abundance is about how common, not how stable.
Relative (percent) abundance.exp: Abundance is how common each isotope is.

Relative (percent) abundance.q: Element Y is 75% Y-35 and 25% Y-37. In 100 atoms of Y, about how many are Y-37?
wrong: 37, since the mass number tells you how many of the hundred atoms there are
Relative (percent) abundance.exp: Relative abundance is the share of atoms: 25% of 100 is 25.

Weighted average atomic mass.q: Element X is 90% X-20 and 10% X-22. Which average mass makes sense?
wrong: That is a plain average; X-20 is far more common.
That treats X-22 as the common one.
That adds the masses without weighting.

Weighted average atomic mass.q: An element is 50% X-10 and 50% X-12. What is its average atomic mass?
wrong: 12, because the heavier isotope always counts more toward the average
That's a sum, not an average.

Isotopic mass.q: In the Candium lab, what did the average mass of one candy type stand for?
wrong: Atomic number is a proton count, not a mass.
The total mixes every type together.
The lab measured masses, not particles.
Isotopic mass.exp: Each candy type was an isotope with its own mass.

Isotopic mass.q: In the Candium lab, why did each candy type get its own average mass?
Isotopic mass.right: Each type stood for one isotope
wrong: Each candy type stood for a different element in the periodic table
All candies were one element, Candium.
To find the number of protons
Isotopic mass.exp: Each candy type played one isotope, and its average mass stood for that isotope's mass.

Ion.q: An atom has 11 protons and 10 electrons. What is it?
wrong: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons.
The protons (11, sodium) did not change.
Ion.exp: Unequal protons and electrons make an ion: Na⁺.

Ion.q: Which change turns a neutral atom into an ion?
wrong: Gaining or losing protons in the nucleus, which changes the atom's charge
That changes the element; ions change electrons.
Ion.exp: An ion has gained or lost electrons; the nucleus doesn't change.

Cation.q: Calcium loses two electrons. What does it become?
wrong: Losing electrons makes it positive, not negative.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons.
It has 2 more protons than electrons now.
Cation.exp: Losing electrons makes a positive ion.

Cation.q: An atom has 20 protons and 18 electrons. What is it?
wrong: An anion with a 2- charge, because it has two more protons than electrons
More protons than electrons means positive.

Anion.q: Sulfur gains two electrons. What does it become?
Anion.exp: Gaining electrons makes a negative ion.

Anion.q: Which of these elements is most likely to form an anion?
wrong: Potassium, since it is very reactive and easily changes its electron count
Anion.exp: Nonmetals gain electrons and form anions.

Why atoms ionize.q: Why does sodium give up an electron to chlorine?
wrong: Na⁺ has a full shell but is still sodium.
Losing an electron makes it slightly lighter.
Why atoms ionize.exp: Na loses 1, Cl gains 1, and both reach complete outer shells.

Why atoms ionize.q: Magnesium gives 2 electrons to oxygen. What do both atoms gain from this?
Why atoms ionize.right: Both end up with complete octets
wrong: Both end up with more protons, which makes them heavier and more stable
They only match a noble gas's electrons.
Why atoms ionize.exp: Atoms ionize to complete their valence shells.

Metals lose, nonmetals gain.q: Potassium and fluorine react. Which one loses electrons?
wrong: Fluorine is a nonmetal; it gains electrons.
One must lose and one must gain.
An ionic bond forms by transfer.
Metals lose, nonmetals gain.exp: Metals lose electrons; nonmetals gain them.

Metals lose, nonmetals gain.q: Calcium and chlorine react. What happens to the electrons?
wrong: Chlorine loses electrons and calcium gains them, since chlorine is on the right
Elements right of the staircase gain.
Metals lose, nonmetals gain.exp: Metals (left) give up electrons; nonmetals (right) take them.

wrong: Gallium is a metal, so it loses electrons.

Group 13 charge.q: Aluminum and oxygen form a compound. What is its formula?
wrong: AlO, since both elements give or take the same number of electrons
Al³⁺ and O²⁻ need a 2:3 ratio.
Group 13 charge.exp: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ cross over to Al₂O₃.

Noble gas charge.q: Which element is least likely to form an ion?
Noble gas charge.exp: Neon's valence shell is already full.

Noble gas charge.q: Which ion has the same electron arrangement as argon, and why doesn't argon itself form ions?
Noble gas charge.right: Cl⁻; argon's shell is already full
wrong: Na⁺, because argon gives away its electrons to sodium to fill its shell
Na⁺ matches neon, and argon doesn't give electrons.
O²⁻ matches neon; mass isn't the reason.
Noble gas charge.exp: Noble gases tend not to form ions because their valence shell is full; Cl⁻ reaches argon's arrangement.

Transition metal charges.q: Which element's ion charge must be given in a problem?
Transition metal charges.exp: Transition metals like iron have variable charges.

Transition metal charges.q: A problem asks for the formula of iron chloride but doesn't give iron's charge. What's wrong?
wrong: Nothing, because iron always forms a +2 ion like the other group 2 metals
Iron is a transition metal with variable charges.
Transition metal charges.exp: Transition metals have variable charges, so a problem must say which one.

Bond.q: What happens to electrons when two atoms form a bond?
wrong: Electrons are not destroyed in a bond.
Bond.exp: A bond is the sharing or giving and taking of electrons.

Bond.q: In table salt, sodium gives an electron to chlorine. In water, H and O share electrons. What do both have in common?
wrong: Both are ionic bonds, because electrons move between the atoms in each case
Salt's electrons are given, not shared.
Bond.exp: A bond is the sharing or giving and taking of electrons.

Ionic bond.q: What holds Na⁺ and Cl⁻ together in table salt?
wrong: Each ion keeps its own nucleus.
Ionic bond.exp: The electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion.

Ionic bond.q: Which pair would form an ionic bond?
wrong: Carbon and oxygen, since both are nonmetals that sit near each other
Noble gases don't bond this way.
Ionic bond.exp: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal.

Covalent compound.q: Which pair of elements would form a covalent compound?
wrong: A metal and a nonmetal form an ionic compound.
Calcium is a metal, so this is ionic.
Lithium is a metal, so this is ionic.

Covalent compound.q: Why is CO₂ covalent but NaCl ionic?
Covalent compound.right: C and O are both nonmetals
wrong: CO₂ is a gas and NaCl is a solid, and only solids can form ionic bonds
Covalent compound.exp: Covalent compounds form between nonmetals; ionic between a metal and a nonmetal.

Chemical formula.q: How many oxygen atoms are in one unit of Al₂O₃?
wrong: 2 is the number of aluminum atoms.
5 is the total number of atoms.

Chemical formula.q: How many atoms in total are in one unit of Ca(NO₃)₂?
wrong: 5, counting one calcium, one nitrogen and three oxygen atoms in the unit
The 2 doubles everything in the parentheses.
That doubles the nitrogen but not the oxygen.
That doubles the oxygen but not the nitrogen.

Ionic formula rule.q: Is MgCl a correct formula? Why or why not?
wrong: Order is right, but the charges must cancel too.
The metal does go first; the problem is the charge.
OK₂, because you can write the ions of an ionic compound in either order
Ionic formula rule.exp: Cation first, and the charges must add to zero: two K⁺ and one O²⁻.

Crossover method.q: Use the crossover method for Al³⁺ and O²⁻. What is the formula?
wrong: The charges were not crossed: each ion takes the other's number.
+3 and -2 do not cancel one to one.
That reduces wrong; Al₂O₂ has +6 and -4.

Crossover method.q: Use the crossover method for Ca²⁺ and O²⁻. What is the final formula?
wrong: Ca₂O₂, because each charge becomes the other ion's subscript exactly
Crossover method.exp: Crossing gives Ca₂O₂, which reduces to CaO.

Polyatomic ion.q: Why is Ca(CN)₂ written with parentheses?
wrong: The 2 applies only to what is inside the parentheses.
Ca(CN)₂ is ionic; parentheses group the ion.
Charges are not written in the formula.
Polyatomic ion.exp: The 2 means two whole CN⁻ ions.

Polyatomic ion.q: Why is Mg(OH)₂ written with parentheses?
wrong: To show that the magnesium is bonded to the oxygen more strongly than hydrogen
To show OH is an element
Polyatomic ion.exp: A polyatomic ion stays together; parentheses show more than one of it.

Properties of ionic compounds.q: Solid salt does not conduct electricity, but salt water does. Why?
Properties of ionic compounds.exp: Dissolved or melted, the ions are free to move.

Properties of ionic compounds.q: An unknown solid has a very high melting point, shatters when hit and conducts only when dissolved. What is it most likely?
wrong: A metal, because metals melt at high temperatures and conduct electricity
Metals conduct as solids and bend.
Properties of ionic compounds.exp: Ionic compounds are brittle, melt at high temperatures and conduct when melted or dissolved.

Molar mass.q: What is the molar mass of water, H₂O? (H = 1.008, O = 16.00)
What is the molar mass of NaCl? (Na = 22.99, Cl = 35.45)
wrong: 12.46 g/mol, found by subtracting the smaller mass from the larger one

Molar mass with subscripts.q: In CaCl₂, how many times do you add chlorine's mass?
wrong: The subscript 2 means two Cl atoms.
3 is the total number of atoms.
Chlorine is part of the formula.
Molar mass with subscripts.exp: Multiply Cl's mass by its subscript, 2.

Molar mass with subscripts.q: What is the molar mass of CO₂? (C = 12.01, O = 16.00)
wrong: 28.01 g/mol, adding the mass of one carbon and the mass of one oxygen

Molar mass with parentheses.q: How many oxygen atoms are in one unit of Ca(NO₃)₂?
wrong: The 2 outside the parentheses doubles the 3 inside.
That adds 3 and 2 instead of multiplying.
2 is the number of NO₃ groups.

Molar mass with parentheses.q: What is the molar mass of Mg(OH)₂? (Mg = 24.31, O = 16.00, H = 1.008)
wrong: 41.32 g/mol, adding one magnesium, one oxygen and one hydrogen together

Mole.q: You have 1 mole of water molecules. How many molecules is that?
wrong: 18.02 is the mass of a mole in grams, not a count.
A mole is a huge count, not one particle.
3 is the atoms in one molecule.

Mole.q: Which contains more particles: 1 mole of helium atoms or 1 mole of water molecules?
wrong: The water, because each water molecule is much heavier than a helium atom
Mass doesn't change the count in a mole.
A mole is the same count for anything.
Mole.exp: A mole is a counting unit: 6.022 × 10²³ particles of anything.

Avogadro's number.q: How many atoms are in 2.00 mol of copper?
wrong: That divides by 2 instead of multiplying.

Avogadro's number.q: How many molecules are in 0.500 mol of CO₂?
wrong: 1.204 × 10²⁴, multiplying Avogadro's number by two instead of by a half

Grams to moles.q: How many moles are in 36.04 g of water (18.02 g/mol)?
wrong: That divides molar mass by grams.
That is the molar mass, not the moles.

Grams to moles.q: How many moles are in 11.69 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol)?
wrong: 683.2 mol, multiplying the mass by the molar mass instead of dividing
That's molar mass ÷ mass, upside down.

Subscript ratio.q: How many moles of H atoms are in 3 mol of CH₄?
wrong: That is the moles of CH₄, not H.
That is per 1 mol of CH₄.
Subscript ratio.exp: 3 mol × 4 H per CH₄ = 12 mol H.

Subscript ratio.q: How many moles of O atoms are in 2 mol of Al₂O₃?
wrong: 4 mol, because aluminum oxide has two aluminum atoms in each formula unit
Subscript ratio.exp: 2 mol × 3 O per unit = 6 mol O.

Roadmap to atoms.q: To go from grams of a compound to number of atoms, what comes first?
wrong: That comes last, after moles of atoms.
That comes after you have moles.
That only finds the molar mass.
Roadmap to atoms.exp: Grams → moles → moles of atoms → atoms.

Roadmap to atoms.q: You know the moles of a compound and want the number of one element's atoms. Which steps come next?
wrong: ÷ molar mass, then × 6.022 × 10²³, the same steps you use when starting from grams
You already have moles; no molar mass step.
Roadmap to atoms.exp: Moles of compound × subscript = moles of the element, then × Avogadro's number = atoms.

Formula unit.q: Why do we count NaCl in formula units, not molecules?
wrong: NaCl has two ions per unit.
Molecules are covalent; NaCl is ionic.
Formula unit.exp: Ionic compounds are counted in formula units.

Formula unit.q: Which substance is counted in formula units rather than molecules?
wrong: H₂O, because it is made of more than one kind of atom bonded together
Formula unit.exp: Ionic compounds like CaCl₂ are counted in formula units.

Boron family.q: Gallium is in group 13. Which family is that?
wrong: Families are named for the top element; boron is at the top of group 13.

Boron family.q: Aluminum is in the boron family. What compound does it form with chlorine?
wrong: AlCl, because aluminum and chlorine each form an ion with a charge of one
Boron family.exp: The boron family forms +3 ions, so Al³⁺ needs three Cl⁻.

Carbon family.q: Silicon is in group 14. Which family is that?
wrong: Families are named for the top element; carbon is at the top of group 14.

Carbon family.q: A quiz asks for the ion charge of carbon-family elements. What does your card say?
wrong: +3, the same as the boron family that sits right next to it on the table
Carbon family.exp: Column 14 has no single ion charge to memorize (4+ or 4-).

Nitrogen family.q: Phosphorus is in group 15. Which family is that?
wrong: Families are named for the top element; nitrogen is at the top of group 15.

Nitrogen family.q: Phosphorus and magnesium form an ionic compound. What is its formula?
wrong: MgP, since both elements are close to each other in the third row of the table
Mg²⁺ and P³⁻ need a 3:2 ratio.
Nitrogen family.exp: Nitrogen family forms -3 ions; Mg²⁺ and P³⁻ cross over to Mg₃P₂.

Oxygen family.q: Sulfur is in group 16. Which family is that?
wrong: Families are named for the top element; oxygen is at the top of group 16.

Oxygen family.q: Sodium and sulfur form a compound. What is its formula?
wrong: NaS, because sodium and sulfur each give or take only one electron here
Oxygen family.exp: The oxygen family forms -2 ions, so two Na⁺ balance one S²⁻.

Hydrogen-1.q: How many neutrons are in ordinary hydrogen-1?
wrong: 3 would be mass number 4, not hydrogen-1.

Hydrogen-1.q: Hydrogen-1 is the only common atom with which feature?
wrong: No protons in its nucleus, so its mass comes from the electron alone
Hydrogen-1.exp: Hydrogen-1 has 1 proton and no neutrons.

Deuterium.q: Deuterium is hydrogen-2. How many neutrons does it have?

wrong: Tritium has one more proton, which is why it has a higher mass number
Deuterium.exp: Deuterium: 1 p, 1 n (mass 2). Tritium: 1 p, 2 n (mass 3).

Tritium.q: How many neutrons are in tritium (hydrogen-3)?
What is the mass number of tritium?
wrong: 2, because tritium has two particles in its nucleus besides its electron

Group 1 charge.q: Lithium is in group 1. What ion does it form?
wrong: Metals lose electrons, so the ion is positive.
Lithium loses 1 electron rather than gaining 7.

Group 1 charge.q: Rubidium is in group 1. What compound does it form with chlorine?
wrong: RbCl₂, because rubidium is a large atom and can hold more chlorine atoms
Group 1 charge.exp: Group 1 forms +1 ions; Rb⁺ + Cl⁻ = RbCl.

Group 2 charge.q: What is the formula of the ion barium forms?
wrong: 1+ is for group 1; barium is in group 2.

Group 2 charge.q: How many electrons does a calcium atom lose when it forms its ion?
wrong: 1, the same number that sodium and the other group 1 metals lose
Group 2 charge.exp: Alkaline earth metals lose 2 valence electrons to form +2 ions.

wrong: Nitrogen is a nonmetal; it gains electrons.

Group 15 charge.q: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. Why does it form N³⁻?
wrong: It loses 3 electrons, which leaves it with a positive charge of three
It gains, so the charge is negative.

Group 16 charge.q: Selenium is in group 16. What ion does it form?
wrong: Selenium is a nonmetal; it gains electrons.

Group 16 charge.q: Calcium and sulfur form a compound. What is its formula?
wrong: CaS₂, because sulfur needs two calcium atoms to balance its charge
Iodine is a nonmetal; it gains electrons.

Group 17 charge.q: Magnesium and fluorine form a compound. What is its formula?
wrong: MgF, since magnesium and fluorine each have a charge of one on their ions
Mg is 2+, so it needs two F⁻.

Carbon-12.q: A carbon atom has 6 neutrons. Which isotope is it?
wrong: The name uses the mass number (6 + 6 = 12), not the neutron count.

Carbon-12.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 differ in mass number by 2. Why?
wrong: Carbon-14 has 2 more protons, so it is heavier than carbon-12 by two
Electrons don't add to mass number.

Carbon-13.q: How many neutrons are in carbon-13?
wrong: That adds 13 and 6 instead of subtracting.
⁶₁₃C, with the mass number written at the bottom and the atomic number on top
7 is the neutron count, not the mass number.
Carbon-13.exp: Mass number 13 on top, atomic number 6 below.

Carbon-14.q: How many neutrons are in carbon-14?
wrong: That adds 14 and 6 instead of subtracting.

Carbon-14.q: A carbon atom has mass number 14. How many protons and neutrons does it have?
wrong: 8 protons and 6 neutrons, since the larger number is always the protons

Oxygen-16.q: How many neutrons are in oxygen-16?

wrong: ⁸₁₆O, with the atomic number written on top and the mass number below
Oxygen-16.exp: Mass number 16 on top, atomic number 8 below.

Oxygen-17.q: An oxygen atom has 9 neutrons. Which isotope is it?
wrong: The name uses the mass number (8 + 9 = 17), not the neutron count.

Oxygen-17.q: How many electrons does a neutral oxygen-17 atom have?
wrong: 9, the same as its neutron count, since neutrons and electrons are paired
Oxygen-17.exp: A neutral atom has electrons equal to its protons: 8.

Oxygen-18.q: What do oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 have different numbers of?
wrong: Both have 8 protons; that's what makes them oxygen.

Oxygen-18.q: How many neutrons are in oxygen-18?
wrong: 18, because the number after the hyphen counts the neutrons directly
